section.title: The Man Born Blind
section.sectionRationale: The sixth sign, the healing of a man born blind, becomes an extended drama of growing sight and deepening blindness. As the once-blind man sees more and more clearly who Jesus is, from the man called Jesus, to a prophet, to one from God, to Lord, the religious leaders grow more and more blind, until they cast him out. Jesus finds the outcast, receives his worship, and pronounces the great reversal: He came so that the blind may see and those who claim to see may go blind.
section.thesis: Jesus, the light of the world, gives sight to a man born blind and, through the man's rising confession and the leaders' hardening rejection, exposes the deeper truth that spiritual sight is given to those who come to Him in faith, while those who proudly claim to see remain in their guilt.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the healing and the question of whose sin caused the blindness; the neighbors' astonishment; the Pharisees' interrogation and the parents' fear; the man's bold second testimony and his expulsion; and Jesus finding him, receiving his worship, and declaring the judgment of sight and blindness.

units.label: The sixth sign
units.note: that the works of God might be displayed

verses.text: Now as Jesus was passing by, He saw a man blind from birth,
and His disciples asked Him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.
While it is daytime, we must do the works of Him who sent Me. Night is coming, when no one can work.
While I am in the world, I am the {{phos|light}} of the world.”
When Jesus had said this, He spit on the ground, made some mud, and applied it to the man’s eyes.
Then He told him, “Go, wash in the Pool of {{siloam|Siloam}}” (which means “Sent”). So the man went and washed, and came back seeing.

units.label: The neighbors astonished
units.note: isn't this the man who used to beg?

verses.text: At this, his neighbors and those who had formerly seen him begging began to ask, “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?”
Some claimed that he was, but others said, “No, he just looks like him.” But the man kept saying, “I am the one.”
“How then were your eyes opened?” they asked.
He answered, “The man they call Jesus made some mud and anointed my eyes, and He told me to go to Siloam and wash. So I went and washed and received my sight.”
“Where is He?” they asked. “I do not know,” he answered.
They brought to the Pharisees the man who had been blind.
Now the day on which Jesus had made the mud and opened his eyes was a Sabbath.
So the Pharisees also asked him how he had received his sight. The man answered, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see.”

Because of this, some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, for He does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How can a sinful man perform such {{semeion|signs}}?” And there was division among them.
So once again they asked the man who had been blind, “What do you say about Him, since it was your eyes He opened?” “He is a prophet,” the man replied.
The Jews still did not believe that the man had been blind and had received his sight until they summoned his parents
and asked, “Is this your son, the one you say was born blind? So how is it that he can now see?”
His parents answered, “We know he is our son, and we know he was born blind.
But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him. He is old enough to speak for himself.”
His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews. For the Jews had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue.
That was why his parents said, “He is old enough. Ask him.”

units.label: One thing I know: I was blind, now I see
units.note: the bold testimony and the expulsion

verses.text: So a second time they called for the man who had been blind and said, “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.”
He answered, “Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!”
“What did He do to you?” they asked. “How did He open your eyes?”
He replied, “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become His disciples?”
Then they heaped insults on him and said, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses.
We know that God spoke to Moses, but we do not know where this man is from.”
“That is remarkable indeed!” the man said. “You do not know where He is from, and yet He opened my eyes.
We know that God does not listen to sinners, but He does listen to the one who worships Him and does His will.
Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind.
If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.”
They replied, “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?” And they threw him out.

units.label: Spiritual blindness
units.note: the blind see and those who see go blind

verses.text: When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, He found the man and said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”
“Who is He, Sir?” he replied. “Tell me so that I may believe in Him.”
“You have already seen Him,” Jesus answered. “He is the One speaking with you.”
“Lord, I {{pisteuo|believe}},” he said. And he worshiped Jesus.
Then Jesus declared, “For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.”
Some of the Pharisees who were with Him heard this, and they asked Him, “Are we blind too?”
“If you were blind,” Jesus replied, “you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.”

phos.gloss: Light. Jesus repeats the claim from the previous chapter, I am the light of the world, and then enacts it by giving light to eyes that had never seen. The physical healing is a parable of the spiritual sight He gives; those who come to the light see, while those who reject it are left in darkness they will not admit.

siloam.gloss: Siloam, the name of the pool, which John notes means Sent. The evangelist highlights the meaning because Jesus is the Sent One, the one sent from the Father; the man is healed by washing in the pool named Sent, a quiet sign that healing comes through the One God has sent. The pool's waters were drawn for the Tabernacles ceremony behind the earlier living water sayings.

semeion.gloss: Sign. Even some Pharisees recognize that such a sign, opening the eyes of a man born blind, could not be done by a mere sinner. The sign points beyond itself to Jesus' identity as the one from God, though the leaders finally refuse to read it rightly. The whole Gospel is built on signs meant to lead to faith.

pisteuo.gloss: To believe, trust. The man's journey is a journey into faith: from knowing only the name of Jesus to confessing Lord, I believe, and worshiping Him. Belief in John is not mere opinion but a whole-person trust that bows before Christ, and it is the fitting response to the light He gives, in contrast to the leaders' proud refusal.

basic.context: Jesus sees a man blind from birth. His disciples ask whose sin caused it; Jesus says neither, but that God's works will be displayed in him, and then, as the light of the world, He heals him with mud and a washing at the pool called Sent. What follows is a long, almost comic drama of investigation. The neighbors are baffled, the Pharisees interrogate the man twice, his frightened parents defer to him, and the man grows steadily bolder in his testimony until the leaders throw him out. Jesus finds the outcast, reveals Himself, receives his worship, and declares that He came so the blind would see and the self-assured would go blind.
basic.hermeneutics: Watch the two opposite journeys. The blind man moves from ignorance to worship, seeing more and more clearly who Jesus is. The leaders move from investigation to insult to expulsion, growing blinder as they claim to see. The key question is not the cause of suffering but the purpose God works through it, and the deeper theme is spiritual sight and blindness. Jesus turns the whole episode into a judgment: those who admit their blindness receive sight, while those who insist they see remain guilty.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on light and sight. Jesus is the phos, the light of the world, and heals through the pool of Siloam, which John notes means Sent, quietly pointing to Jesus as the Sent One. Some Pharisees admit no mere sinner could do such a semeion, a sign, yet they will not believe. The healed man, by contrast, comes to pisteuo, to believe, confessing Lord, I believe, and worshiping.
basic.typology: The washing in the pool named Sent points to cleansing and sight given through the One sent from God. The giving of sight to the blind fulfills the messianic promises of Isaiah, a sign of the age of salvation dawning in Jesus.
basic.christ: Christ is the light of the world who gives sight, the Son of Man who receives worship, and the judge whose coming divides the seeing from the blind. He seeks out the man who was cast out, showing that He gathers those the religious establishment rejects.
basic.god: God works His purposes even through lifelong suffering, so that His works may be displayed. He is not the author of the man's blindness as punishment; He is the one who turns it to glory. He listens to those who worship Him and do His will.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 35 and 42 promise that the eyes of the blind will be opened. John 8:12 declares the light of the world. 2 Corinthians 4 speaks of God shining light into blind hearts. John 3 said light divides those who come and those who hide.
basic.oneStory: The promised opening of blind eyes arrives in Jesus, the light of the world and the Sent One. As one poor beggar is given sight and led to worship while the proud are left in darkness, the story shows how the coming of the light divides humanity, gathering the humble who admit their need and hardening those who trust their own vision.

context.literary:
John 9 is the most carefully staged narrative in the Gospel, a courtroom drama in seven short scenes: the disciples and Jesus, verses 1 to 7; the neighbours, 8 to 12; the Pharisees' first inquiry, 13 to 17; the parents, 18 to 23; the Pharisees' second inquiry, 24 to 34; and Jesus and the man again, 35 to 41. The healing itself takes only two verses, and everything else is its aftermath. John gives the miracle a line and the argument about it thirty-five.

The structure is a mirror. At the start Jesus is outside with the man. At the centre, in the interrogations, Jesus is absent altogether and the man stands alone. At the end Jesus returns and the two are together again. The man's journey is the reverse of the leaders'. He begins by calling Jesus 'the man they call Jesus', verse 11, moves to 'a prophet', verse 17, then to one who must be 'from God', verse 33, and ends with 'Lord, I believe', verse 38. The Pharisees begin with a division, 'there was division among them', verse 16, move to fixed hostility, verse 24, then to insult, verse 28, and finally to expulsion, verse 34.

Irony does most of the work. The people who see cannot see, and the man who could not see sees through them. The Pharisees insist, 'We know that this man is a sinner', verse 24, and the man answers with the one thing he knows. When they claim, 'We know that God spoke to Moses', verse 29, the man turns their own logic against them in verses 30 to 33, a short syllogism the experts cannot answer. The repeated word 'know' runs through the chapter, and in the end the man knows the one thing that matters while the leaders, who claim to know everything, are exposed in verse 41.

The chapter is also a hinge. It continues the light of the world theme of 8:12 and leads straight into the shepherd discourse of chapter 10, where the thieves who drove out the man are the false shepherds.
context.historical:
The scene probably follows the Feast of Tabernacles of chapters 7 and 8, since Jesus still speaks of Himself as the light of the world. Jerusalem is crowded and the temple area is full of beggars. In that world blindness was a common affliction and the blind had no way to earn a living except by begging, which is how the neighbours knew this man, verse 8. Being born blind added a particular sorrow, for a person who has never seen has no hope of explanation.

The disciples' question in verse 2 reflects a common assumption that suffering is a sign of sin. The Law spoke of the sins of parents being visited on children, Exodus 20:5, and some teachers of the time even imagined that a child might sin in the womb. Yet Scripture itself pushed back: Job's friends were wrong to link every pain to guilt, Job 4:7-8 and 42:7, and Jesus elsewhere rejects the idea that the victims of a disaster were worse sinners, Luke 13:2-5. The disciples' question is natural and Jesus' answer is a turning point.

The healing method is unusual. Saliva and clay were used for eyes in the ancient world, and Jesus uses saliva in Mark 7:33 and 8:23, but here the clay is paired with a command to go to the pool of Siloam. The pool, fed by the tunnel Hezekiah cut to bring water within the city walls, 2 Kings 20:20, lay at the southern end of the city, and the man had to make his way to it with mud on his eyes. The Mishnah records later rabbinic regulations on the Sabbath that restricted kneading and the treatment of eyes. John tells us the healing happened on a Sabbath, verse 14, so the leaders' complaint about Sabbath breaking has a legal edge.

The fear of the parents in verse 22 is the key historical detail. Confessing Jesus as the Christ would get a person put out of the synagogue. The Greek word aposynagogos appears in the New Testament only in John, here, in 12:42 and in 16:2. To be put out was to lose community, trade and religious standing. Many readers think this reflects the situation of John's own church as well as the day of Jesus.
context.canonical:
The prophets had made the opening of blind eyes a sign of God's coming salvation. 'Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped,' Isaiah 35:5. The Servant is given 'to open the eyes of the blind', Isaiah 42:7, and Isaiah 29:18 and 42:18 say the same. The Psalms praise the LORD as the one who gives sight to the blind, Psalm 146:8. In the Old Testament no case of a man healed of congenital blindness is recorded, which is why the man in verse 32 says that never before has anyone heard of it. Jesus' act is therefore not only a healing but a sign that the promised age has begun, and in Matthew 11:5 He points John the Baptist's disciples to the same sign.

The theme of blind leaders also has a long history. The shepherds of Israel in Ezekiel 34 were condemned for failing the weak, and Isaiah 56:10 calls Israel's watchmen blind. In Isaiah 6:9-10, which John quotes in 12:39-40, the people are told to keep hearing but not understanding, seeing but not perceiving. Chapter 9 is the clearest narrative of this: those who see in the ordinary sense cannot see the sign in front of them.

The New Testament carries the chapter forward. Paul says God has shone in believers' hearts, 'to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ', 2 Corinthians 4:6, and also that the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, 2 Corinthians 4:4. The risen Lord tells Paul that he is sent to open eyes, 'to turn them from darkness to light', Acts 26:18. In Revelation 3:17-18 the Laodiceans think they see and are told to buy salve for their eyes, a direct echo of verse 41. The early church also came to speak of baptism as illumination, which draws on this chapter.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants the reader to occupy the man's place and then ask which of the two groups they are in. The sign is given so that we will ask what we do when the Lord does something we cannot explain away. The chapter is a pastoral lesson about bearing witness under pressure. The man has no theological training and little power, and he is questioned by the most learned men in the city. Yet his short, honest answers, 'I was blind, but now I see', verse 25, and the plain logic of verses 30 to 33 are more than a match for the experts. John's readers, who knew the threat of the synagogue ban, were meant to take heart from a man who told the truth at a cost.

John also meant to correct a false and cruel reading of suffering. Jesus' first word is a refusal to assign blame, and His next word is that His followers must work while it is day, verse 4. Suffering is neither a puzzle to be solved nor a verdict to be pronounced; it is an occasion for the works of God.

Finally, John meant the chapter's last exchange to land with force. Those who say 'we see' are told that their guilt remains. It is possible to be religious, informed and confident and still be in the dark, and that possibility is the warning the whole chapter has been preparing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what happened to one man and one set of leaders. Healing by mud and a pool is something Jesus did and not a method He commanded His followers to copy. Nowhere in the Gospels are disciples told to make clay for the eyes. The sign belongs to the unique ministry of the light of the world, and its meaning lies in what it shows about Him, not in a ritual to repeat.

Several things do carry forward as direct instruction. The refusal of verse 3 to blame the sufferer is a standing rule for how believers speak to the sick, the disabled and the grieving. It does not forbid asking hard questions, but it forbids pronouncing a cause that God has not given. The command of verse 4, 'we must do the works of Him who sent Me', is addressed to the disciples as well as to Jesus, and the 'we' makes it ours. And the example of the healed man, who tells what he knows, answers the questions he can, admits what he does not know and will not be bullied into denying what he has experienced, is plainly meant to be followed.

The leaders' behaviour is descriptive, not a model. The expulsion of the man is shown as a failure, not as a pattern of church discipline. Reading the passage as a guide to discipline gets it backwards, since the ones who throw him out are the blind ones. The chapter also does not teach that every disability is a special occasion for a miracle. It teaches that no disability is evidence of the sufferer's guilt, and that God can display His works in the midst of it.

debates.question: What exactly does Jesus say about the purpose of the man's blindness in verse 3?

views.label: The blindness was so that God's works would be displayed
views.case: The BSB reads, 'Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.' The purpose clause is attached to the condition. God permitted and directed this life toward a day of display, so that the man's whole history becomes the stage for the healing. This is the natural reading of the words and it fits the Old Testament pattern that God directs even affliction to His ends, as with Joseph, Genesis 50:20.

views.label: A different division of the sentences, joining the purpose to verse 4
views.case: The earliest Greek manuscripts have no marks to divide the sentences, so some have taken the purpose clause with verse 4: 'but so that the works of God may be displayed in him, we must work the works of Him who sent Me while it is day.' On this reading Jesus is saying nothing about why the man was born blind, only about what the disciples must do now that they have met him. It avoids the suggestion that God caused the blindness for the sake of a later display.

debates.bearing: Both readings reject the disciples' assumption that someone's sin caused this, and both direct attention to God's works and not to blame. The first is the more common reading and fits Paul's confidence that God works in all things. The second guards against saying that God inflicts suffering for show. Either way the verse should never be used to tell a sufferer that their pain is God's performance.

debates.question: How can Jesus say He came 'for judgment' when He also says He did not come to judge?

views.label: Different senses of judgment
views.case: John 3:17 says God did not send the Son to condemn the world, and 12:47 says He did not come to judge the world but to save it. In 9:39 Jesus uses the word krima, which refers to a verdict or a sorting. His coming does not aim at condemnation, but it inevitably divides, as light divides those who come from those who hide, John 3:19-21. The judgment is the result of people's response to Him.

views.label: A judgment that is also reversal
views.case: The statement is shaped like the prophetic reversals, in which the lowly are lifted and the proud brought low, as in Mary's song in Luke 1:51-53. Jesus' coming turns the ordinary order upside down: the one who admits blindness is given sight and the one who claims sight is left blind. The judgment is God's act of overturning false confidence.

debates.bearing: The two views fit together. The Son does not come to condemn, yet His presence exposes what is in people and sorts them according to their response. Verse 41 makes it plain that the dividing line is the admission of need, not the possession of sight.

study.originalLanguages:
The first Greek word to notice is pelos, the clay or mud of verses 6, 11, 14 and 15. John uses the word four times, and it is the material of a potter's work, which is why many readers hear an echo of the creation of Adam from the dust of the ground, Genesis 2:7. John does not say so, so the link is a suggestion, not a certainty. It is still striking that the light of the world makes mud, as the Creator once made man from dust, in order to complete what was missing in a man born blind.

The name Siloam is the second. John says it means 'Sent', and the Hebrew name Shiloach is from the verb shalach, 'to send'. Isaiah 8:6 speaks of 'the gently flowing waters of Shiloah' that the people rejected. The Greek verbs of sending that fill John, apostello and pempo, are used of Jesus again and again in 9:4 and elsewhere, so the pool's name quietly points to the one the Father sent. The man is sent to the Sent One's pool and comes back seeing.

The word for 'judgment' in verse 39 is krima, a decision or verdict, and not the word krisis that John uses in 3:19 for the process of judging. The shade of difference is slight, but it suggests the outcome, the sentence, that His coming brings.

The Pharisees' demand in verse 24, 'Give glory to God!', is not a request for praise. It is a formula for solemn confession, and the closest Old Testament parallel is Joshua's call to Achan, 'give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him', Joshua 7:19. In effect they are saying, 'Swear to tell the truth,' and the truth they want is that Jesus is a sinner.

The word hamartia, sin, is the engine of the chapter. It appears in the disciples' question, the Pharisees' accusation, the man's reply, and finally in the last verse, where Jesus says that those who claim to see keep their sin. The way the single word shifts hands from the sufferer to the accuser to the one who says 'we see' is the best summary of the chapter's reversal.

Finally, ekballo, 'to throw out', appears in verse 34 for what the leaders do to the man, and again in verse 35. It is the same verb used of the driving out of demons and of the cleansing of the temple. The ones who claim to guard God's house throw out one whom He has healed.

typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 8:6 describes the waters of Shiloah as flowing gently and as rejected by a people who would rather trust human powers. The pool whose name means Sent is now the place where a blind man washes and sees, while the leaders reject the one who sent him there. The correspondence is that quiet water from God is refused by those who trust other strengths. The escalation is that the waters of Shiloah in Isaiah's day were a picture of the Lord's gentle rule, and here the Sent One Himself brings sight. The type falls short because the pool heals only because Jesus commands the washing; the water has no power in itself.

typology.type: Creation from dust and the new creation
typology.fulfillment: The Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground, Genesis 2:7, and Jesus forms eyes with clay. The text does not claim this link, so it should be held lightly, but the New Testament does describe the new life as a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17, and says that the God who said 'Let light shine out of darkness' has shone in our hearts, 2 Corinthians 4:6. What the Creator once did to make the first man, He does here to restore one man's sight. The correspondence is real as a pattern but falls short as a proof: the passage gives no explicit sign that John intended a deliberate echo.

typology.type: Naaman and the washing at the river
typology.fulfillment: Naaman was told to wash seven times in the Jordan, 2 Kings 5:10, and he was healed only when he obeyed a command that seemed ordinary to him. The blind man likewise is told to wash in a pool and is healed as he obeys. Both stories show that healing comes through the word of God's messenger and that obedience, not the water, is the means. Jesus Himself refers to Naaman in Luke 4:27. The escalation is that Elisha only sent a messenger while Jesus is Himself the sent One. The type falls short in its scope: Naaman's skin was cleansed, but the man of John 9 receives sight and then worships.

typology.type: The Servant who opens blind eyes
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 42:7 says the Servant will open the eyes of the blind and bring prisoners from the dungeon. The healing of the man born blind is the Servant's work in action. Matthew 12:17-21 explicitly connects Jesus' healings with Isaiah 42, and Luke 4:18 quotes Isaiah 61 about recovering of sight for the blind. The correspondence is that Jesus does what the Servant was promised to do, and the escalation is that He does it for one who has never seen, a case beyond ordinary cure. The sign also shows the larger mission, since the Servant's work reaches the heart as well as the eye, as the man's confession shows.

study.christ:
Christ appears in this chapter as the light, the sent one, the one who finds and the one who judges. As the light He claims in verse 5 to be what the world lacks, and He proves it by giving sight where there was none. The saying is hedged by 'while I am in the world', which looks ahead to His departure and to the work His disciples must do. At the cross the light seems to go out, but the resurrection shows that the light cannot be extinguished, John 1:5.

As the sent one, He is placed beside the pool whose name means Sent. The Father's mission is not an abstract idea; it is something the man must actually walk to and wash in. The man's obedience to a strange command is a small picture of the faith the Gospel asks of all.

As the one who finds, He seeks out the man after the leaders have thrown him out, verse 35. There is nothing in the man's behaviour that earns this. Jesus finds him because the man has suffered for telling the truth, and so the Lord finds those whom the world casts out for His sake, as He promised in Luke 6:22-23. The picture matches the good shepherd of the next chapter, who calls His own by name and leads them out, John 10:3. And then Jesus reveals Himself plainly: 'You have already seen Him. He is the One speaking with you,' verse 37. The man had seen Jesus' face before, but only now sees who He is.

As the judge, Jesus says that He has come 'for judgment', and the chapter shows what that means. He gives sight to those who know they are blind and leaves in darkness those who say they see. The Son of Man, who in Daniel 7:13-14 receives authority and in John 5:27 is given authority to judge, is here seen carrying out that sorting in the plainest way. His presence divides without His uttering a sentence.

The man's final act is worship, and Jesus accepts it. In a Gospel that takes pains to show Jesus refusing glory for Himself, His readiness here to be worshiped is remarkable. Angels and apostles refuse worship, Acts 10:25-26 and Revelation 19:10, but Jesus does not. The man's confession 'Lord, I believe' is the pattern for the confession of Thomas in John 20:28.

A caution keeps the chapter honest. The details of the mud and the pool need not be turned into a code. The link to Christ is secure because of what the text says about the light and the sent one, and because the New Testament uses the same language of sight and blindness for Christ's work, 2 Corinthians 4:4-6.
study.god:
The doctrine of God that this chapter shapes begins with a refusal. God is not the author of arbitrary punishments, and suffering is not a coded verdict on the sufferer. Jesus' answer to the disciples says that nothing in the man's life is outside God's purpose, yet it does not make God the cause of sin or the maker of cruelty. This holds two things together that the disciples could not: that God is sovereign over affliction, and that He is not a tyrant who assigns pain to the guilty. The book of Job had said the same, and Jesus now says it in a living case.

God is also the one who works. 'We must do the works of Him who sent Me,' verse 4. The Father is active in the world through the Son, and in the Gospel the Father's works are the Son's works, John 5:17-19. The Sabbath controversy is about exactly this. God's rest on the seventh day, Genesis 2:2, did not mean that He ceased to sustain and heal. The man's Sabbath healing shows that the God of the Sabbath is also the God who lifts burdens.

God hears the one who worships Him and does His will. The man's remark that 'God does not listen to sinners, but He does listen to the one who worships Him and does His will', verse 31, echoes Psalm 66:18. It is not a full theology of prayer, since God also hears the cry of the sinner who begs for mercy, Luke 18:13-14, but as a piece of lay reasoning it is sound: a miracle of this kind could not come from one who is against God.

God is the one who reverses. The first become last, the blind see, the sighted go blind. Paul says that God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, 1 Corinthians 1:27, and the chapter shows how: an uneducated beggar silences the council. This is not an accident of the story but the shape of God's way with people. He opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble, James 4:6.

God is patient with unbelief and honest about its cost. The leaders are given every chance, with a sign, a witness, a second hearing and a plain word from Jesus, and still they refuse. Yet God does not leave them unwarned. The final answer in verse 41 is not an insult but a diagnosis, and a diagnosis is the first act of a physician.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to thank the God who has opened our eyes and to stay humble before Him. Our sight is a gift, and to say 'we see' as a claim to independence is the one answer that leaves guilt in place. The right prayer is that of the man, 'Lord, I believe', and then to bow.

crossReferences.note: Jesus' claim at the Feast of Tabernacles that He is the light of the world is repeated in 9:5. The two chapters belong together: the first states the claim and the second shows it in action in a man's eyes.

The prophet promised that the eyes of the blind would be opened when God came to save His people. The healing of the man born blind is a sign that this day has come, and Jesus later points John the Baptist's disciples to the same sign, Matthew 11:5.

The Servant is to open blind eyes and bring prisoners out of darkness. John 9 shows the Servant doing it, and John 8:12 and 9:5 show the same Servant as the light, which is the other half of the same chapter in Isaiah, 42:6.

The prophet says the people rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah. John's note that Siloam means Sent and his story of a man sent there to wash puts the pool in the foreground again. Those who reject the waters of Shiloah are the very leaders who reject the man healed there.

Jesus refuses to say that victims of a massacre and a fallen tower were worse sinners than others. It parallels His answer in John 9:3, and together the two passages close off the easy equation of suffering with guilt.

Joshua's call to Achan, 'give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him', explains the formula in verse 24. The leaders use a solemn oath of confession, intended to make the man swear that Jesus is a sinner.

The psalmist says that if he had cherished iniquity in his heart, the Lord would not have listened. The man's argument in verse 31 uses the same principle: a man who works such a sign cannot be an enemy of God.

Paul says that the god of this age has blinded unbelievers' minds, and that God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts. The two halves, blindness and gift of sight, are the doctrine behind the story of the man and the leaders.

Jesus says that light has come into the world and people loved darkness because their deeds were evil. This anticipates the sorting of chapter 9: the man comes toward the light and the leaders hold back from it.

The Laodiceans say that they are rich and need nothing, not knowing that they are wretched and blind. They are told to buy eye salve so that they can see. The warning is the same as verse 41: self-confident sight is the worst blindness.

The good shepherd calls His own sheep by name and leads them out, and they follow because they know His voice. Having been thrown out by the leaders, the man is found by the shepherd, and the next chapter explains what it means.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with light that God speaks into the dark and ends with a city without a night, so the question of who can see runs through the whole. In Genesis 3 the eyes of the man and woman are opened, but what they see is their own nakedness and shame, verse 7. It is a seeing that is really a kind of blindness, a clarity about the wrong things. From then on the human problem is not a lack of information but a darkened heart. Isaiah's complaint that the people see and do not perceive, Isaiah 6:9-10, runs through the Old Testament, and the promise of the new covenant answers it with the removal of the blindness, Isaiah 29:18 and 35:5.

Israel's history is the story of a people entrusted with light who were meant to bring it to the nations, Isaiah 49:6, and whose leaders so often failed. Ezekiel's shepherds fed themselves and neglected the sheep, and in John 9 the leaders drive out the one sheep who has been healed. The chapter takes the old story of faithless shepherds and a blind people and sets it in a single street in Jerusalem.

In the middle of the story stands the man himself, as small as can be, a beggar with no name. He is a picture of everyone whom the light finds. He does not seek the light; the light comes to him, makes mud and sends him. He does not understand all that is happening, and he is put out of the community for his honesty. Yet at the end he worships. This is the pattern of the gospel in miniature, and it is the pattern of the church that will be formed among those who are put out for the sake of the name.

The story is finished in the new creation. 'There will be no more night in the city, and they will have no need for the light of a lamp or of the sun. For the Lord God will shine on them,' Revelation 22:5, and His servants 'will see His face', Revelation 22:4. The man who was blind from birth, who first saw the face of Jesus in the temple area, is the picture of a people whose eyes have been opened for good. In that city the Pharisees' question, 'Are we blind too?', has been answered for ever, and the answer for the humble is that they will see.

quiz.q: How does Jesus answer the question of who sinned to cause the man's blindness?

options.text: Neither the man nor his parents; it happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.
options.note: Verse 3 rejects the blame and points to God's purpose.

options.text: The man himself sinned before birth.
options.note: Jesus explicitly says neither the man nor his parents sinned to cause it.

options.text: His parents' sin was the cause.
options.note: This was a common assumption of the day, but Jesus rejects it; the blindness was not punishment for their sin.

options.text: No one's sin caused it, and God had a purpose in it.
options.note: True in substance, but it omits the specific goal, that the works of God would be displayed in him.

quiz.q: How does the healed man's understanding of Jesus develop through the chapter?

options.text: From the man called Jesus, to a prophet, to one from God, to Lord whom he worships.
options.note: His confession grows through the interrogations until he believes and worships.

options.text: He believes fully and completely from the very first moment.
options.note: His faith grows step by step; he does not begin with full understanding.

options.text: He never really decides who Jesus is.
options.note: He ends by confessing Lord, I believe, and worshiping Jesus.

options.text: He comes to call Jesus a prophet and one from God.
options.note: True of the middle of his journey, but it stops short of his final confession and worship.

quiz.q: What was the man's simple, unshakable testimony to the Pharisees?

options.text: One thing I know: I was blind, but now I see.
options.note: Verse 25 records his plain, powerful witness.

options.text: He mainly retold how Jesus had put mud on his eyes and healed him.
options.note: He did recount what happened, but his boldest and simplest testimony was the plain fact, I was blind, now I see.

options.text: He admitted he was not sure anything had changed.
options.note: He was certain: I was blind, but now I see.

options.text: He insisted that Jesus must be from God to do such a thing.
options.note: He does argue this later, but his simplest testimony is the personal fact, I was blind, now I see.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by coming for judgment so the blind see and the seeing go blind?

options.text: Those who admit their blindness receive sight, while those who proudly claim to see remain guilty.
options.note: Verses 39 to 41 explain the reversal in terms of humility and pride.

options.text: Jesus came mainly to condemn the world.
options.note: His coming does bring judgment, but John 3:17 says He came to save; condemnation is not His chief purpose.

options.text: Physical blindness is a sign of God's rejection.
options.note: The chapter teaches the opposite; the physically blind man is the one who truly sees.

options.text: His coming divides people by how they respond to the light.
options.note: True, but it omits the sharp point that the proud who claim to see are left in guilt.

quiz.q: Why were the man's parents afraid to speak about the healing?

options.text: Because anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue.
options.note: Verse 22 gives the reason, fear of excommunication.

options.text: Because they preferred that their grown son speak for himself.
options.note: They did say he is old enough, ask him, but John tells us the real reason was fear of being put out of the synagogue.

options.text: Because they doubted he had been healed.
options.note: They confirmed the facts; it was fear of the leaders that made them defer to him.

options.text: Because they feared the religious authorities.
options.note: True, but it does not name the specific threat, being put out of the synagogue for confessing Christ.

questions: The disciples wanted to know whose fault the blindness was; Jesus pointed instead to what God would do through it. How might God be at work in a hardship you are tempted only to blame?
The healed man simply said, I was blind, but now I see. What is the plain, personal testimony of what Jesus has done in your life?
Under pressure the man grew bolder while his parents grew silent. Where is fear of others' disapproval keeping you from speaking honestly about Jesus?
Jesus sought out the man after he was thrown out. How does it comfort you that Christ draws near to those rejected by others?
The proud who claimed to see stayed blind. Where might a confident sense that you already see be keeping you from seeing Jesus more truly?

translationNotes.note: Siloam means Sent, as John notes; the detail points to Jesus as the Sent One from the Father, through whom sight and cleansing come.
Do you believe in the Son of Man; the BSB footnote records a variant, the Son of God, in some manuscripts. Either title calls the man to faith in Jesus.
Being put out of the synagogue was a severe penalty of exclusion; John's note reflects the sharp conflict between the synagogue and confessors of Christ.
The BSB footnote gives the literal wording and notes that some manuscripts do not include the man's words Lord, I believe, and his worship in verses 38 and 39a; the sense of the passage is unchanged.
